blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define inflation, define deflation, and tell a change in the general price level from a change in one price.

blocks.heading: Two directions of the general price level
blocks.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of an economy over a period, usually a year: prices on average rise, and a unit of money buys fewer goods than before. Deflation is the mirror image: a sustained fall in the general price level over a period, where prices on average fall and a unit of money buys more. Both are statements about the general level - the cost of the whole basket of goods and services a typical household buys - and neither describes a single good. A steady 4% yearly rise in prices and the long period of gently falling prices Japan lived through are the two directions of the same measurement.

blocks.heading: A rise in one price is not inflation
blocks.text: The boundary: a single price can rise while the general level is steady, because other prices may hold or fall. Bread becoming dearer at a Katutura market stall after a poor wheat harvest is a rise in one price; it becomes inflation where the rise spreads until the whole basket costs more than before. The test: ask what happened to the general price level, not to one good. A second boundary learners cross: a slower rise in prices is not deflation. Where prices rise 4% a year and then 2% a year, the general level is still rising, more slowly; deflation needs the level itself to fall, as when a price index falls from 120.0 to 117.6 - the level has fallen, not merely its rate of rise.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The value of money is what these definitions turn on: money itself is built in topic 3.1 and the price stability aim in topic 4.2. The index that measures the general level is built in the next section.
